entries.8889931a025ad705dbc350a04f988e1521e97f03: <div sID="gen2402" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="13" osisID="Lev.13" sID="Lev.13"/> <div eID="gen2402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2403" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2404" type="x-p"/> The next ceremonial uncleanness is that of the leprosy, concerning which the law was very large and particular; we have the discovery of it in this chapter, and the cleansing of the leper in the next. Scarcely any one thing in all the levitical law takes up so much room as this. I. Rules are here given by which the priest must judge whether the man had the leprosy or no, according as the symptom was that appeared. 1. If it was a swelling, a scab, or a bright spot, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.1-Lev.13.17">ver. 1-17</reference>. 2. If it was a bile, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.18-Lev.13.23">ver. 18-23</reference>. 3. If it was in inflammation, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.24-Lev.13.28">ver. 24-28</reference>. 4. If it was in the head or beard, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.29-Lev.13.37">ver. 29-37</reference>. 5. If it was a bright spot, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.38-Lev.13.39">ver. 38, 39</reference>. 6. If it was in a bald head, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.40-Lev.13.44">ver. 40-44</reference>. II. Direction is given how the leper must be disposed of, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.45-Lev.13.46">ver. 45, 46</reference>. III. Concerning the leprosy in garments, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.47-Lev.13.59">ver. 47</reference>, &c.
entries.df6cb9a6053a0befda093a49ffb89901578c273b: <div eID="gen2404" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2403" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Law Concerning Leprosy. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2405" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses and Aaron, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> When a man shall have in the skin of his flesh a rising, a scab, or bright spot, and it be in the skin of his flesh <hi type="italic">like</hi> the plague of leprosy; then he shall be brought unto Aaron the priest, or unto one of his sons the priests: <hi type="super">3</hi> And the priest shall look on the plague in the skin of the flesh: and <hi type="italic">when</hi> the hair in the plague is turned white, and the plague in sight <hi type="italic">be</hi> deeper than the skin of his flesh, it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a plague of leprosy: and the priest shall look on him, and pronounce him unclean. <hi type="super">4</hi> If the bright spot <hi type="italic">be</hi> white in the skin of his flesh, and in sight <hi type="italic">be</hi> not deeper than the skin, and the hair thereof be not turned white; then the priest shall shut up <hi type="italic">him that hath</hi> the plague seven days: <hi type="super">5</hi> And the priest shall look on him the seventh day: and, behold, <hi type="italic">if</hi> the plague in his sight be at a stay, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the plague spread not in the skin; then the priest shall shut him up seven days more: <hi type="super">6</hi> And the priest shall look on him again the seventh day: and, behold, <hi type="italic">if</hi> the plague <hi type="italic">be</hi> somewhat dark, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the plague spread not in the skin, the priest shall pronounce him clean: it <hi type="italic">is but</hi> a scab: and he shall wash his clothes, and be clean. <hi type="super">7</hi> But if the scab spread much abroad in the skin, after that he hath been seen of the priest for his cleansing, he shall be seen of the priest again: <hi type="super">8</hi> And <hi type="italic">if</hi> the priest see that, behold, the scab spreadeth in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a leprosy. <hi type="super">9</hi> When the plague of leprosy is in a man, then he shall be brought unto the priest; 10 And the priest shall see <hi type="italic">him</hi>: and, behold, <hi type="italic">if</hi> the rising <hi type="italic">be</hi> white in the skin, and it have turned the hair white, and <hi type="italic">there be</hi> quick raw flesh in the rising; <hi type="super">11</hi> It <hi type="italic">is</hi> an old leprosy in the skin of his flesh, and the priest shall pronounce him unclean, and shall not shut him up: for he <hi type="italic">is</hi> unclean. <hi type="super">12</hi> And if a leprosy break out abroad in the skin, and the leprosy cover all the skin of <hi type="italic">him that hath</hi> the plague from his head even to his foot, wheresoever the priest looketh; <hi type="super">13</hi> Then the priest shall consider: and, behold, <hi type="italic">if</hi> the leprosy have covered all his flesh, he shall pronounce <hi type="italic">him</hi> clean <hi type="italic">that hath</hi> the plague: it is all turned white: he <hi type="italic">is</hi> clean. <hi type="super">14</hi> But when raw flesh appeareth in him, he shall be unclean. <hi type="super">15</hi> And the priest shall see the raw flesh, and pronounce him to be unclean: <hi type="italic">for</hi> the raw flesh <hi type="italic">is</hi> unclean: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a leprosy. <hi type="super">16</hi> Or if the raw flesh turn again, and be changed unto white, he shall come unto the priest; <hi type="super">17</hi> And the priest shall see him: and, behold, <hi type="italic">if</hi> the plague be turned into white; then the priest shall pronounce <hi type="italic">him</hi> clean <hi type="italic">that hath</hi> the plague: he <hi type="italic">is</hi> clean. <div eID="gen2405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2406" type="x-p"/> I. Concerning the plague of leprosy we may observe in general, 1. That it was rather an uncleanness than a disease; or, at least, so the law considered it, and therefore employed not the physicians but the priests about it. Christ is said to cleanse lepers, not to cure them. We do not read of any that died of the leprosy, but it rather buried them alive, by rendering them unfit for conversation with any but such as were infected like themselves. Yet there is a tradition that Pharaoh, who sought to kill Moses, was the first that ever was struck with this disease, and that he died of it. It is said to have begun first in Egypt, whence it spread into Syria. It was very well known to Moses, when he put his own hand into his bosom and took it out leprous. 2. That it was a plague inflicted immediately by the hand of God, and came not from natural causes, as other diseases; and therefore must be managed according to a divine law. Miriam's leprosy, and Gehazi's, and king Uzziah's, were all the punishments of particular sins: and, if generally it was so, no marvel there was so much care taken to distinguish it from a common distemper, that none might be looked upon as lying under this extraordinary token of divine displeasure but those that really were so. 3. That it is a plague not now known in the world; what is commonly called the leprosy is of a quite different nature. This seems to have been reserved as a particular scourge for the sinners of those times and places. The Jews retained the idolatrous customs they had learnt in Egypt, and therefore God justly caused this with some others of the diseases of Egypt to follow them. Yet we read of Naaman the Syrian, who was a leper, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.1">2 Kings v. 1</reference>. 4. That there were other breakings-out in the body which did very much resemble the leprosy, but were not it, which might make a man sore and loathsome and yet not ceremonially unclean. Justly are our bodies called vile bodies, which have in them the seeds of so many diseases, by which the lives of so many are made bitter to them. 5. That the judgment of it was referred to the priests. Lepers were looked upon as stigmatized by the justice of God, and therefore it was left to his servants the priests, who might be presumed to know his mark best, to pronounce who were lepers and who were not. All the Jews say, "Any priest, though disabled by a blemish to attend the sanctuary, might be a judge of the leprosy, provided the blemish were not in his eye. And he might" (they say) "take a common person to assist him in the search, but the priest only must pronounce the judgment." 6. That it was a figure of the moral pollution of men's minds by sin, which is the leprosy of the soul, defiling to the conscience, and from which Christ alone can cleanse us; for herein the power of his grace infinitely transcends that of the legal priesthood, that the priest could only convict the leper (for by the law is the knowledge of sin), but Christ can cure the leper, he can take away sin. <hi type="italic">Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean,</hi> which was more than the priests could do, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.2">Matt. viii. 2</reference>. Some think that the leprosy signified, not so much sin in general as a state of sin, by which men are separated from God (their spot not being the spot of God's children), and scandalous sin, for which men are to be shut out from the communion of the faithful. It is a work of great importance, but of great difficulty, to judge of our spiritual state: we have all cause to suspect ourselves, being conscious to ourselves of sores and spots, but whether clean or unclean is the question. A man might have a scab (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.6">v. 6</reference>) and yet be clean: the best have their infirmities; but, as there were certain marks by which to know that it was a leprosy, so there are characters of such as are in the gall of bitterness, and the work of ministers is to declare the judgment of leprosy and to assist those that suspect themselves in the trial of their spiritual state, remitting or retaining sin. And hence the keys of the kingdom of heaven are said to be given to them, because they are to separate between the precious and the vile, and to judge who are fit as clean to partake of the holy things and who as unclean must be debarred from them. <div eID="gen2406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2407" type="x-p"/> II. Several rules are here laid down by which the judgment of the priest must be governed. 1. If the sore was but <hi type="italic">skin-deep,</hi> it was to be hoped it was not the <hi type="italic">leprosy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.13.4">v. 4</reference>. But, if it was <hi type="italic">deeper than the skin,</hi> the man must be pronounced unclean, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.3">v. 3</reference>. The infirmities that consist with grace do not sink deep into the soul, but <hi type="italic">the mind</hi> still <hi type="italic">serves the law of God,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">inward man delights in it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.7.22">Rom. vii. 22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.25">25</reference>. But if the matter be really worse than it shows, and the inwards be infected, the case is dangerous. 2. If the sore <hi type="italic">be at a stay,</hi> and do not <hi type="italic">spread,</hi> it is no leprosy, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.4-Lev.13.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. But if it <hi type="italic">spread much abroad,</hi> and continue to do so after several inspections, the case is bad, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.7-Lev.13.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. If men do not grow worse, but a stop be put to the course of their sins and their corruptions be checked, it is to be hoped they will grow better; but if sin get ground, and they become worse every day, they are going downhill. 3. If there was <hi type="italic">proud raw flesh</hi> in the rising, the priest needed not to wait any longer, it was certainly a leprosy, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.10-Lev.13.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. Nor is there any surer indication of the badness of a man's spiritual state than the heart's rising in self-conceit, confidence in the flesh, and resistance of the reproofs of the word and strivings of the Spirit. 4. If the eruption, whatever it was, <hi type="italic">covered all the skin</hi> from head to foot, it was no leprosy (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.12-Lev.13.13">v. 12, 13</reference>); for it was an evidence that the vitals were sound and strong, and nature hereby helped itself, throwing out what was burdensome and pernicious. There is hope in the small-pox when they come out well: so if men freely confess their sins, and hide them not, there is no danger comparable to theirs that cover their sins. Some gather this from it, that there is more hope of the profane than of hypocrites. The publicans and harlots went into the kingdom of heaven before scribes and Pharisees. In one respect, the sudden breakings-out of passion, though bad enough, are not so dangerous as malice concealed. Others gather this, that, if we judge ourselves, we shall not be judged; if we see and own that there is <hi type="italic">no health in us, no soundness in our flesh,</hi> by reason of sin, we shall <hi type="italic">find grace in the eyes of the Lord.</hi> 5. The priest must take time in making his judgment, and not give it rashly. If the matter looked suspicious, he must shut up the patient seven days, and then seven days more, that his judgment might be <hi type="italic">according to truth.</hi> This teaches all, both ministers and people, not to be hasty in their censures, nor to judge any thing <hi type="italic">before the time.</hi> If <hi type="italic">some men's sins go before unto judgment,</hi> the sins of others <hi type="italic">follow after,</hi> and so men's good works; therefore let nothing be done <hi type="italic">suddenly,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.22">1 Tim. v. 22</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.24">24</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.25">25</reference>. 6. If the person suspected was found to be clean, yet he must <hi type="italic">wash his clothes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.6">v. 6</reference>), because he had been under the suspicion, and there had been in him that which gave ground for the suspicion. Even the prisoner that is acquitted must go down on his knees. We have need to be washed in the blood of Christ from our spots, though they be not leprosy-spots; for who can say, <hi type="italic">I am pure from sin?</hi> though there are those who through grace are <hi type="italic">innocent from the great transgression.</hi>
entries.d35e88ceb87cdef2670a57380049df1a5d792e7c: <div eID="gen2407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2408" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> The flesh also, in which, <hi type="italic">even</hi> in the skin thereof, was a boil, and is healed, <hi type="super">19</hi> And in the place of the boil there be a white rising, or a bright spot, white, and somewhat reddish, and it be showed to the priest; <hi type="super">20</hi> And if, when the priest seeth it, behold, it <hi type="italic">be</hi> in sight lower than the skin, and the hair thereof be turned white; the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a plague of leprosy broken out of the boil. <hi type="super">21</hi> But if the priest look on it, and, behold, <hi type="italic">there be</hi> no white hairs therein, and <hi type="italic">if</hi> it <hi type="italic">be</hi> not lower than the skin, but <hi type="italic">be</hi> somewhat dark; then the priest shall shut him up seven days: <hi type="super">22</hi> And if it spread much abroad in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a plague. <hi type="super">23</hi> But if the bright spot stay in his place, <hi type="italic">and</hi> spread not, it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a burning boil; and the priest shall pronounce him clean. <hi type="super">24</hi> Or if there be <hi type="italic">any</hi> flesh, in the skin whereof <hi type="italic">there is</hi> a hot burning, and the quick <hi type="italic">flesh</hi> that burneth have a white bright spot, somewhat reddish, or white; <hi type="super">25</hi> Then the priest shall look upon it: and, behold, <hi type="italic">if</hi> the hair in the bright spot be turned white, and it <hi type="italic">be in</hi> sight deeper than the skin; it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a leprosy broken out of the burning: wherefore the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> the plague of leprosy. <hi type="super">26</hi> But if the priest look on it, and, behold, <hi type="italic">there be</hi> no white hair in the bright spot, and it <hi type="italic">be</hi> no lower than the <hi type="italic">other</hi> skin, but <hi type="italic">be</hi> somewhat dark; then the priest shall shut him up seven days: <hi type="super">27</hi> And the priest shall look upon him the seventh day: <hi type="italic">and</hi> if it be spread much abroad in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> the plague of leprosy. <hi type="super">28</hi> And if the bright spot stay in his place, <hi type="italic">and</hi> spread not in the skin, but it <hi type="italic">be</hi> somewhat dark; it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a rising of the burning, and the priest shall pronounce him clean: for it <hi type="italic">is</hi> an inflammation of the burning. <hi type="super">29</hi> If a man or woman have a plague upon the head or the beard; <hi type="super">30</hi> Then the priest shall see the plague: and, behold, if it <hi type="italic">be</hi> in sight deeper than the skin; <hi type="italic">and there be</hi> in it a yellow thin hair; then the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a dry scall, <hi type="italic">even</hi> a leprosy upon the head or beard. <hi type="super">31</hi> And if the priest look on the plague of the scall, and, behold, it <hi type="italic">be</hi> not in sight deeper than the skin, and <hi type="italic">that there is</hi> no black hair in it; then the priest shall shut up <hi type="italic">him that hath</hi> the plague of the scall seven days: <hi type="super">32</hi> And in the seventh day the priest shall look on the plague: and, behold, <hi type="italic">if</hi> the scall spread not, and there be in it no yellow hair, and the scall <hi type="italic">be</hi> not in sight deeper than the skin; <hi type="super">33</hi> He shall be shaven, but the scall shall he not shave; and the priest shall shut up <hi type="italic">him that hath</hi> the scall seven days more: <hi type="super">34</hi> And in the seventh day the priest shall look on the scall: and, behold, <hi type="italic">if</hi> the scall be not spread in the skin, nor <hi type="italic">be</hi> in sight deeper than the skin; then the priest shall pronounce him clean: and he shall wash his clothes, and be clean. 35 But if the scall spread much in the skin after his cleansing; <hi type="super">36</hi> Then the priest shall look on him: and, behold, if the scall be spread in the skin, the priest shall not seek for yellow hair; he <hi type="italic">is</hi> unclean. <hi type="super">37</hi> But if the scall be in his sight at a stay, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> there is black hair grown up therein; the scall is healed, he <hi type="italic">is</hi> clean: and the priest shall pronounce him clean. <div eID="gen2408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2409" type="x-p"/> The priest is here instructed what judgment to make if there was any appearance of a leprosy, either, 1. In an old ulcer, or bile, that has been healed, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.18">v. 18</reference>, &c. When old sores, that seemed to be cured, break out again, it is to be feared there is a leprosy in them; such is the danger of those who, having escaped the pollutions of the world, are again <hi type="italic">entangled therein and overcome.</hi> Or, 2. In a burn by accident, for this seems to be meant, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.24">v. 24</reference>, &c. The burning of strife and contention often proves the occasion of the rising up and breaking out of that corruption which witnesses to men's faces that they are unclean. 3. In a scall-head. And in this commonly the judgment turned upon a very small matter. If the hair in the scall was black, it was a sign of soundness; if yellow, it was an indication of a leprosy, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.30-Lev.13.37">v. 30-37</reference>. The other rules in these cases are the same with those mentioned before. In reading of these several sorts of ailments, it will be good for us, 1. To lament the calamitous state of human life, which lies exposed to so many grievances. What troops of diseases are we beset with on every side! and they all entered by sin. 2. To give thanks to God if he has never afflicted us with any of these sores: if the constitution is healthful, and the body lively and easy, we are bound to glorify God with our bodies.
entries.99dcbf4e4349233fd230daeab122ccff3f087029: <div eID="gen2409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2410" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">38</hi> If a man also or a woman have in the skin of their flesh bright spots, <hi type="italic">even</hi> white bright spots; <hi type="super">39</hi> Then the priest shall look: and, behold, <hi type="italic">if</hi> the bright spots in the skin of their flesh <hi type="italic">be</hi> darkish white; it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a freckled spot <hi type="italic">that</hi> groweth in the skin; he <hi type="italic">is</hi> clean. 40 And the man whose hair is fallen off his head, he <hi type="italic">is</hi> bald; <hi type="italic">yet is</hi> he clean. <hi type="super">41</hi> And he that hath his hair fallen off from the part of his head toward his face, he <hi type="italic">is</hi> forehead bald: <hi type="italic">yet is</hi> he clean. <hi type="super">42</hi> And if there be in the bald head, or bald forehead, a white reddish sore; it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a leprosy sprung up in his bald head, or his bald forehead. <hi type="super">43</hi> Then the priest shall look upon it: and, behold, <hi type="italic">if</hi> the rising of the sore <hi type="italic">be</hi> white reddish in his bald head, or in his bald forehead, as the leprosy appeareth in the skin of the flesh; <hi type="super">44</hi> He is a leprous man, he <hi type="italic">is</hi> unclean: the priest shall pronounce him utterly unclean; his plague <hi type="italic">is</hi> in his head. <hi type="super">45</hi> And the leper in whom the plague <hi type="italic">is,</hi> his clothes shall be rent, and his head bare, and he shall put a covering upon his upper lip, and shall cry, Unclean, unclean. <hi type="super">46</hi> All the days wherein the plague <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> in him he shall be defiled; he <hi type="italic">is</hi> unclean: he shall dwell alone; without the camp <hi type="italic">shall</hi> his habitation <hi type="italic">be.</hi> <div eID="gen2410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2411" type="x-p"/> We have here, <div eID="gen2411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2412" type="x-p"/> I. Provisos that neither a <hi type="italic">freckled skin</hi> nor a <hi type="italic">bald head</hi> should be mistaken for a leprosy, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.38-Lev.13.41">v. 38-41</reference>. Every deformity must not forthwith be made a ceremonial defilement. Elisha was jeered for his <hi type="italic">bald head</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.23">2 Kings ii. 23</reference>); but it was the children of Bethel, that knew not the judgments of their God, who turned it to his reproach. <div eID="gen2412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2413" type="x-p"/> II. A particular brand set upon the leprosy if at any time it did appear in a <hi type="italic">bald head: The plague is in his head, he is utterly unclean,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.13.44">v. 44</reference>. If the leprosy of sin have seized the head, if the judgment be corrupted, and wicked principles which countenance and support wicked practices, be embraced, it is an <hi type="italic">utter uncleanness,</hi> from which few are ever cleansed. Soundness in the faith keeps the leprosy from the head, and saves conscience from being shipwrecked. <div eID="gen2413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2414" type="x-p"/> III. Directions what must be done with the convicted leper. When the priest, upon mature deliberation, had solemnly pronounced him unclean, <div eID="gen2414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2415" type="x-p"/> 1. He must pronounce himself so, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.45">v. 45</reference>. He must put himself into the posture of a mourner and cry, <hi type="italic">Unclean, unclean.</hi> The leprosy was not itself a sin, but it was a sad token of God's displeasure and a sore affliction to him that was under it. It was a reproach to his name, put a full stop to his business in the world, cut him off from conversation with his friends and relations, condemned him to banishment till he was cleansed, shut him out from the sanctuary, and was, in effect, the ruin of all the comfort he could have in this world. Heman, it would seem, either was a leper or alludes to the melancholy condition of a leper, <reference osisRef="Ps.88.8-Ps.88.18">Ps. lxxxviii. 8</reference>, &c. He must therefore, (1.) Humble himself under the mighty hand of God, not insisting upon his cleanness when the priest had pronounced him unclean, but justifying God and accepting the <hi type="italic">punishment of his iniquity.</hi> He must signify this by <hi type="italic">rending his clothes, uncovering</hi> his head, and <hi type="italic">covering his upper lip,</hi> all tokens of shame and confusion of face, and very significant of that self-loathing and self-abasement which should fill the hearts of penitents, the language of which is self-judging. Thus must we take to ourselves the shame that belongs to us, and with broken hearts call ourselves by our own name, <hi type="italic">Unclean, unclean</hi>—heart unclean, life unclean, unclean by original corruption, unclean by actual transgression—unclean, and therefore worthy to be for ever excluded from communion with God, and all hope of happiness in him. <hi type="italic">We are all as an unclean thing</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.64.6">Isa. lxiv. 6</reference>)—unclean, and therefore undone, if infinite mercy do not interpose. (2.) He must give warning to others to take heed of coming near him. Wherever he went, he must cry to those he saw at a distance, "<hi type="italic">I am unclean, unclean,</hi> take heed of touching me." Not that the leprosy was catching, but by the touch of a leper ceremonial uncleanness was contracted. Every one therefore was concerned to avoid it; and the leper himself must give notice of the danger. And this was all that the law could do, in that it was weak through the flesh; it taught the leper to cry, <hi type="italic">Unclean, unclean,</hi> but the gospel has put another cry into the lepers' mouths, <reference osisRef="Luke.17.12-Luke.17.13">Luke xvii. 12, 13</reference>, where we find ten lepers crying with a loud voice, <hi type="italic">Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.</hi> The law only shows us our disease; the gospel shows us our help in Christ. <div eID="gen2415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2416" type="x-p"/> 2. He must then be shut out of the camp, and afterwards, when they came to Canaan, out of the city, town, or village, where he lived, and <hi type="italic">dwell alone</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.46">v. 46</reference>), associating with none but those that were lepers like himself. When king Uzziah became a leper, he was banished from his palace, and <hi type="italic">dwelt in a separate house,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.21">2 Chron. xxvi. 21</reference>. And see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.7.3">2 Kings vii. 3</reference>. This typified the purity which ought to be preserved in the gospel church, by the solemn and authoritative exclusion of scandalous sinners, that hate to be reformed, from the communion of the faithful. <hi type="italic">Put away from among yourselves that wicked person,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.13">1 Cor. v. 13</reference>.
entries.4a69c71f06a1db8be5f9ec7b1256e5838ad52bb5: <div eID="gen2416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2417" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">47</hi> The garment also that the plague of leprosy is in, <hi type="italic">whether it be</hi> a woollen garment, or a linen garment; 48 Whether <hi type="italic">it be</hi> in the warp, or woof; of linen, or of woollen; whether in a skin, or in any thing made of skin; <hi type="super">49</hi> And if the plague be greenish or reddish in the garment, or in the skin, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in any thing of skin; it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a plague of leprosy, and shall be showed unto the priest: <hi type="super">50</hi> And the priest shall look upon the plague, and shut up <hi type="italic">it that hath</hi> the plague seven days: <hi type="super">51</hi> And he shall look on the plague on the seventh day: if the plague be spread in the garment, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in a skin, <hi type="italic">or</hi> in any work that is made of skin; the plague <hi type="italic">is</hi> a fretting leprosy; it <hi type="italic">is</hi> unclean. <hi type="super">52</hi> He shall therefore burn that garment, whether warp or woof, in woollen or in linen, or any thing of skin, wherein the plague is: for it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a fretting leprosy; it shall be burnt in the fire. <hi type="super">53</hi> And if the priest shall look, and, behold, the plague be not spread in the garment, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in any thing of skin; <hi type="super">54</hi> Then the priest shall command that they wash <hi type="italic">the thing</hi> wherein the plague <hi type="italic">is,</hi> and he shall shut it up seven days more: <hi type="super">55</hi> And the priest shall look on the plague, after that it is washed: and, behold, <hi type="italic">if</hi> the plague have not changed his colour, and the plague be not spread; it <hi type="italic">is</hi> unclean; thou shalt burn it in the fire; it <hi type="italic">is</hi> fret inward, <hi type="italic">whether</hi> it <hi type="italic">be</hi> bare within or without. <hi type="super">56</hi> And if the priest look, and, behold, the plague <hi type="italic">be</hi> somewhat dark after the washing of it; then he shall rend it out of the garment, or out of the skin, or out of the warp, or out of the woof: <hi type="super">57</hi> And if it appear still in the garment, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in any thing of skin; it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a spreading <hi type="italic">plague</hi>: thou shalt burn that wherein the plague <hi type="italic">is</hi> with fire. <hi type="super">58</hi> And the garment, either warp, or woof, or whatsoever thing of skin <hi type="italic">it be,</hi> which thou shalt wash, if the plague be departed from them, then it shall be washed the second time, and shall be clean. <hi type="super">59</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the law of the plague of leprosy in a garment of woollen or linen, either in the warp, or woof, or any thing of skins, to pronounce it clean, or to pronounce it unclean. <div eID="gen2417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2418" type="x-p"/> This is the law concerning the plague of leprosy in a garment, whether linen or woollen. A leprosy in a garment, with discernible indications of it, the colour changed by it, the garment fretted, the nap worn off, and this in some one particular part of the garment, and increasing when it was shut up, and not to be got out by washing is a thing which to us now is altogether unaccountable. The learned confess that it was a sign and a miracle in Israel, an extraordinary punishment inflicted by the divine power, as a token of great displeasure against a person or family. 1. The process was much the same with that concerning a leprous person. The garment suspected to be tainted was not to be burnt immediately, though, it may be, there would have been no great loss of it; for in no case must sentence be given merely upon a surmise, but it must be <hi type="italic">shown to the priest.</hi> If, upon search, it was found that there was a <hi type="italic">leprous spot</hi> (the Jews say no bigger than a bean), it must be <hi type="italic">burnt,</hi> or at least that part of the garment in which the spot was, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.52">v. 52</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.57">57</reference>. If the cause of the suspicion was gone, it must be <hi type="italic">washed,</hi> and then might be used, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.58">v. 58</reference>. 2. The signification also was much the same, to intimate the great malignity there is in sin: it not only defiles the sinner's conscience, but it brings a stain upon all his employments and enjoyments, all he has and all he does. <hi type="italic">To those that are defiled and unbelieving is nothing pure,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.1.15">Tit. i. 15</reference>. And we are taught hereby to hate even <hi type="italic">the garments spotted with the flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.23">Jude 23</reference>. Those that make their clothes servants to their pride and lust may see them thereby tainted with a leprosy, and doomed to the fire, <reference osisRef="Isa.3.18-Isa.3.24">Isa. iii. 18-24</reference>. But the ornament of <hi type="italic">the hidden man of the heart is incorruptible,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.4">1 Pet. iii. 4</reference>. The robes of righteousness never fret nor are moth-eaten.  <chapter eID="Lev.13"/> <div eID="gen2418" type="x-p"/>

entries.e04b6d47ad5ce797cd89071ff7c926ca55e27513: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1084"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 13</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.13.1-Lev.13.59">Le 13:1-59</reference>. The Laws and Tokens in Discerning Leprosy.</title> <div sID="gen1497" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1084"/><hi type="bold">2. When a man shall have in the skin, &c.--</hi>The fact of the following rules for distinguishing the plague of leprosy being incorporated with the Hebrew code of laws, proves the existence of the odious disease among that people. But a short time, little more than a year (if so long a period had elapsed since the exodus) when symptoms of leprosy seem extensively to have appeared among them; and as they could not be very liable to such a cutaneous disorder amid their active journeyings and in the dry open air of Arabia, the seeds of the disorder must have been laid in Egypt, where it has always been endemic. There is every reason to believe that this was the case: that the leprosy was not a family complaint, hereditary among the Hebrews, but that they got it from intercourse with the Egyptians and from the unfavorable circumstances of their condition in the house of bondage. The great excitement and irritability of the skin in the hot and sandy regions of the East produce a far greater predisposition to leprosy of all kinds than in cooler temperatures; and cracks or blotches, inflammations or even contusions of the skin, very often lead to these in Arabia and Palestine, to some extent, but particularly in Egypt. Besides, the subjugated and distressed state of the Hebrews in the latter country, and the nature of their employment, must have rendered them very liable to this as well as to various other blemishes and misaffections of the skin; in the production of which there are no causes more active or powerful than a depressed state of body and mind, hard labor under a burning sun, the body constantly covered with the excoriating dust of brick fields, and an impoverished diet--to all of which the Israelites were exposed while under the Egyptian bondage. It appears that, in consequence of these hardships, there was, even after they had left Egypt, a general predisposition among the Hebrews to the contagious forms of leprosy--so that it often occurred as a consequence of various other affections of the skin. And hence all cutaneous blemishes or blains--especially such as had a tendency to terminate in leprosy--were watched with a jealous eye from the first [Good, Study of Medicine]. A swelling, a pimple, or bright spot on the skin, created a strong ground of suspicion of a man's being attacked by the dreaded disease.<div eID="gen1497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1498" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">then he shall be brought unto Aaron the priest, &c.--</hi>Like the Egyptian priests, the Levites united the character of physician with that of the sacred office; and on the appearance of any suspicious eruptions on the skin, the person having these was brought before the priest--not, however, to receive medical treatment, though it is not improbable that some purifying remedies might be prescribed, but to be examined with a view to those sanitary precautions which it belonged to legislation to adopt. <div eID="gen1498" type="x-p"/>
entries.067c4699e0babbbe2d34f84f73636716bfbf4abd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1085"/><div sID="gen1499" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1085"/><hi type="bold">3-6. the priest shall look on the plague in the skin of the flesh, &c.--</hi>The leprosy, as covering the person with a white, scaly scurf, has always been accounted an offensive blemish rather than a serious malady in the East, unless when it assumed its less common and malignant forms. When a Hebrew priest, after a careful inspection, discovered under the cutaneous blemish the distinctive signs of contagious leprosy, the person was immediately pronounced unclean, and is supposed to have been sent out of the camp to a lazaretto provided for that purpose. If the symptoms appeared to be doubtful, he ordered the person to be kept in domestic confinement for seven days, when he was subjected to a second examination; and if during the previous week the eruption had subsided or appeared to be harmless, he was instantly discharged. But if the eruption continued unabated and still doubtful, he was put under surveillance another week; at the end of which the character of the disorder never failed to manifest itself, and he was either doomed to perpetual exclusion from society or allowed to go at large. A person who had thus been detained on suspicion, when at length set at liberty, was obliged to "wash his clothes," as having been tainted by ceremonial pollution; and the purification through which he was required to go was, in the spirit of the Mosaic dispensation, symbolical of that inward purity it was instituted to promote. <div eID="gen1499" type="x-p"/>
entries.4ea984ce4612eaa162a407d3ce5ffdb0bd738d3f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1086"/><div sID="gen1500" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1086"/><hi type="bold">7-8. But if the scab spread much abroad in the skin--</hi>Those doubtful cases, when they assumed a malignant character, appeared in one of two forms, apparently according to the particular constitution of the skin or of the habit generally. The one was "somewhat dark" [Le 13:6]--that is, the obscure or dusky leprosy, in which the natural color of the hair (which in Egypt and Palestine is black) is not changed, as is repeatedly said in the sacred code, nor is there any depression in the dusky spot, while the patches, instead of keeping stationary to their first size, are perpetually enlarging their boundary. The patient laboring under this form was pronounced unclean by the Hebrew priest or physician, and hereby sentenced to a separation from his family and friends--a decisive proof of its being contagious. <div eID="gen1500" type="x-p"/>
entries.778bc113b74b2c987c9fc883c3c521c049322de3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1087"/><div sID="gen1501" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1087"/><hi type="bold">9-37. if the rising be white--</hi>This BRIGHT WHITE leprosy is the most malignant and inveterate of all the varieties the disease exhibits, and it was marked by the following distinctive signs: A glossy white and spreading scale, upon an elevated base, the elevation depressed in the middle, but without a change of color; the black hair on the patches participating in the whiteness, and the scaly patches themselves perpetually enlarging their boundary. Several of these characteristics, taken separately, belong to other blemishes of the skin as well; so that none of them was to be taken alone, and it was only when the whole of them concurred that the Jewish priest, in his capacity of physician, was to pronounce the disease a malignant leprosy. If it spread over the entire frame without producing any ulceration, it lost its contagious power by degrees; or, in other words, it ran through its course and exhausted itself. In that case, there being no longer any fear of further evil, either to the individual himself or to the community, the patient was declared clean by the priest, while the dry scales were yet upon him, and restored to society. If, on the contrary, the patches ulcerated and quick or fungous flesh sprang up in them, the purulent matter of which, if brought into contact with the skin of other persons, would be taken into the constitution by means of absorbent vessels, the priest was at once to pronounce it an inveterate leprosy. A temporary confinement was them declared to be totally unnecessary, and he was regarded as unclean for life [Dr. Good]. Other skin affections, which had a tendency to terminate in leprosy, though they were not decided symptoms when alone, were: "a boil" (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.18-Lev.13.23">Le 13:18-23</reference>); "a hot burning,"--that is, a fiery inflammation or carbuncle (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.24-Lev.13.28">Le 13:24-28</reference>); and "a dry scall" (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.29-Lev.13.37">Le 13:29-37</reference>), when the leprosy was distinguished by being deeper than the skin and the hair became thin and yellow. <div eID="gen1501" type="x-p"/>
entries.2c7902354d875e74bfa20c1ef8d7975183366d96: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1088"/><div sID="gen1502" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1088"/><hi type="bold">38-39. If a man ... or a woman have in the skin of their flesh bright spots--</hi>This modification of the leprosy is distinguished by a dull white color, and it is entirely a cutaneous disorder, never injuring the constitution. It is described as not penetrating below the skin of the flesh and as not rendering necessary an exclusion from society. It is evident, then, that this common form of leprosy is not contagious; otherwise Moses would have prescribed as strict a quarantine in this as in the other cases. And hereby we see the great superiority of the Mosaic law (which so accurately distinguished the characteristics of the leprosy and preserved to society the services of those who were laboring under the uncontagious forms of the disease) over the customs and regulations of Eastern countries in the present day, where all lepers are indiscriminately proscribed and are avoided as unfit for free intercourse with their fellow men. <div eID="gen1502" type="x-p"/>
entries.5840b5d0d64b962e68c78a321395358a8c233262: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1089"/><div sID="gen1503" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1089"/><hi type="bold">40-41. bald ... forehead bald--</hi>The falling off of the hair, when the baldness commences in the back part of the head, is another symptom which creates a suspicion of leprosy. But it was not of itself a decisive sign unless taken in connection with other tokens, such as a "sore of a reddish white color" [Le 13:43]. The Hebrews as well as other Orientals were accustomed to distinguish between the forehead baldness, which might be natural, and that baldness which might be the consequence of disease. <div eID="gen1503" type="x-p"/>
entries.34730e7658f73242c81d4bcdeec926c01832f084: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1090"/><div sID="gen1504" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1090"/><hi type="bold">45. the leper in whom the plague is, his clothes shall be rent, &c.--</hi>The person who was declared affected with the leprosy forthwith exhibited all the tokens of suffering from a heavy calamity. Rending garments and uncovering the head were common signs of mourning. As to "the putting a covering upon the upper lip," that means either wearing a moustache, as the Hebrews used to shave the upper lip [Calmet], or simply keeping a hand over it. All these external marks of grief were intended to proclaim, in addition to his own exclamation "Unclean!" that the person was a leper, whose company every one must shun. <div eID="gen1504" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d7361df16db8f5c458f3d23d1648bf9083e0445: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1091"/><div sID="gen1505" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1091"/><hi type="bold">46. he shall dwell alone; without the camp--</hi>in a lazaretto by himself, or associated with other lepers (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.7.3">2Ki 7:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.7.8">8</reference>). <div eID="gen1505" type="x-p"/>
entries.d2bd0c73f9671f3f4534f2d7704366543a632c5e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1092"/><div sID="gen1506" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1092"/><hi type="bold">47-59. The garment ... that the ... leprosy is in--</hi>It is well known that infectious diseases, such as scarlet fever, measles, the plague, are latently imbibed and carried by the clothes. But the language of this passage clearly indicates a disease to which clothes themselves were subject, and which was followed by effects on them analogous to those which malignant leprosy produces on the human body--for similar regulations were made for the rigid inspection of suspected garments by a priest as for the examination of a leprous person. It has long been conjectured and recently ascertained by the use of a lens, that the leprous condition of swine is produced by myriads of minute insects engendered in their skin; and regarding all leprosy as of the same nature, it is thought that this affords a sufficient reason for the injunction in the Mosaic law to destroy the clothes in which the disease, after careful observation, seemed to manifest itself. Clothes are sometimes seen contaminated by this disease in the West Indies and the southern parts of America [Whitlaw, Code of Health]; and it may be presumed that, as the Hebrews were living in the desert where they had not the convenience of frequent changes and washing, the clothes they wore and the skin mats on which they lay, would be apt to breed infectious vermin, which, being settled in the stuff, would imperceptibly gnaw it and leave stains similar to those described by Moses. It is well known that the wool of sheep dying of disease, if it had not been shorn from the animal while living, and also skins, if not thoroughly prepared by scouring, are liable to the effects described in this passage. The stains are described as of a greenish or reddish color, according, perhaps, to the color or nature of the ingredients used in preparing them; for acids convert blue vegetable colors into red and alkalis change then into green [Brown]. It appears, then, that the leprosy, though sometimes inflicted as a miraculous judgment (<reference osisRef="Num.12.10">Nu 12:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.27">2Ki 5:27</reference>) was a natural disease, which is known in Eastern countries still; while the rules prescribed by the Hebrew legislator for distinguishing the true character and varieties of the disease and which are far superior to the method of treatment now followed in those regions, show the divine wisdom by which he was guided. Doubtless the origin of the disease is owing to some latent causes in nature; and perhaps a more extended acquaintance with the archæology of Egypt and the natural history of the adjacent countries, may confirm the opinion that leprosy results from noxious insects or a putrid fermentation. But whatever the origin or cause of the disease, the laws enacted by divine authority regarding it, while they pointed in the first instance to sanitary ends, were at the same time intended, by stimulating to carefulness against ceremonial defilement, to foster a spirit of religious fear and inward purity.  <chapter eID="Lev.13"/>

entries.472b013bc2484550bf9f9c5976b114683effe7c3: <div eID="gen4669" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen4670" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4671" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4671" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4670" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4672" type="x-p"/> Laws relative to the leprosy. It is to be known by a rising in the flesh, a scab, or a bright spot, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.1">Lev 13:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.2">Lev 13:2</reference>. When the priest sees these signs he shall pronounce the man unclean, infected with the leprosy, and unfit for society, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.3">Lev 13:3</reference>. Dubious or equivocal signs of this disorder, and how the person is to be treated in whom they appear, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.4-Lev.13.8">Lev 13:4-8</reference>. In what state of this disorder the priest may pronounce a man clean or unclean, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.9-Lev.13.13">Lev 13:9-13</reference>. Of the raw flesh, the sign of the unclean leprosy, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.14">Lev 13:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.15">Lev 13:15</reference>. Of the white flesh, the sign of the leprosy called clean, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.16">Lev 13:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.17">Lev 13:17</reference>. Of the leprosy which succeeds a boil, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.18-Lev.13.20">Lev 13:18-20</reference>. Equivocal marks relative to this kind of leprosy, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.21">Lev 13:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.22">Lev 13:22</reference>. Of the burning boil, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.23">Lev 13:23</reference>. Of the leprosy arising out of the burning boil, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.24">Lev 13:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.25">Lev 13:25</reference>. Equivocal marks relative to this kind of leprosy, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.26-Lev.13.28">Lev 13:26-28</reference>. Of the plague on the head or in the beard, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.29">Lev 13:29</reference>. Of the scall, and how it is to be treated, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.30-Lev.13.37">Lev 13:30-37</reference>. Of the plague of the bright white spots, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.38">Lev 13:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.39">Lev 13:39</reference>. Of the bald head, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.40">Lev 13:40</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.41">Lev 13:41</reference>. Of the white reddish sore in the bald head, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.42-Lev.13.44">Lev 13:42-44</reference>. The leper shall rend his clothes, put a patch on his upper lip, and cry unclean, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.45">Lev 13:45</reference>. He shall be obliged to avoid society, and live by himself without the camp, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.46">Lev 13:46</reference>. Of the garments infected by the leprosy, and the signs of this infection, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.47-Lev.13.52">Lev 13:47-52</reference>. Equivocal marks relative to this infection, and how the garment is to be treated, by washing or by burning, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.53-Lev.13.58">Lev 13:53-58</reference>. Conclusion relative to the foregoing particulars, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.59">Lev 13:59</reference>.
entries.f47cd34b4d7b812f87eebdc0f822396dfdc1861b: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen4672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4673" type="x-p"/> The plague of leprosy - This dreadful disorder has its name leprosy, from the Greek λεποα, from λεπις, a scale, because in this disease the body was often covered with thin white scales, so as to give it the appearance of snow. Hence it is said of the hand of Moses, <reference osisRef="Exo.4.6">Exo 4:6</reference>, that it was leprous as snow; and of Miriam, <reference osisRef="Num.12.10">Num 12:10</reference>, that she became leprous, as white as snow; and of Gehazi, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.27">2Kgs 5:27</reference>, that, being judicially struck with the disease of Naaman, he went out from Elisha's presence a leper as white as snow. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.4.6">Exo 4:6</reference>. In Hebrew this disease is termed צרעת tsaraath, from צרע mor tsara, to smite or strike; but the root in Arabic signifies to cast down or prostrate, and in Ethiopian, to cause to cease, because, says Stockius, "it prostrates the strength of man, and obliges him to cease from all work and labor." There were three signs by which the leprosy was known. <div eID="gen4673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4674" type="x-p"/> 1. A bright spot. <div eID="gen4674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4675" type="x-p"/> 2. A rising (enamelling) of the surface. <div eID="gen4675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4676" type="x-p"/> 3. A scab; the enamelled place producing a variety of layers, or stratum super stratum, of these scales. <div eID="gen4676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4677" type="x-p"/> The account given by Mr. Maundrell of the appearance of several persons whom he saw infected with this disorder in Palestine, will serve to show, in the clearest light, its horrible nature and tendency. "When I was in the Holy Land," says he, in his letter to the Rev. Mr. Osborn, Fellow of Exeter College, "I saw several that labored under Gehazi's distemper; particularly at Sichem, (now Naplosu), there were no less than ten that came begging to us at one time. Their manner is to come with small buckets in their hands, to receive the alms of the charitable; their touch being still held infectious, or at least unclean. The distemper, as I saw it on them, was quite different from what I have seen it in England; for it not only defiles the whole surface of the body with a foul scurf, but also deforms the joints of the body, particularly those of the wrists and ankles, making them swell with a gouty scrofulous substance, very loathsome to look on. I thought their legs like those of old battered horses, such as are often seen in drays in England. The whole distemper, indeed, as it there appeared, was so noisome, that it might well pass for the utmost corruption of the human body on this side the grave. And certainly the inspired penman could not have found out a fitter emblem, whereby to express the uncleanness and odiousness of vice." - Maundrell's Travels. Letters at the end. The reader will do well to collate this account with that given from Dr. Mead; see the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.4.6">Exo 4:6</reference> (note).
entries.065e88b464c09ea55bc7b41079414846af433f5c: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen4677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4678" type="x-p"/> The priest shall - pronounce him unclean - וטמא אתו vetimme otho; literally, shall pollute him, i. e., in the Hebrew idiom, shall declare or pronounce him polluted; and in <reference osisRef="Lev.13.23">Lev 13:23</reference>, it is said, the priest shall pronounce him clean, וטהרו הכהן vetiharo haccohen, the priest shall cleanse him, i. e., declare him clean. In this phrase we have the proper meaning of <reference osisRef="Mat.16.19">Mat 16:19</reference> : Whatsoever ye bind on earth, shall be bound in heaven; and whatsoever ye loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven. By which our Lord intimates that the disciples, from having the keys, i. e., the true knowledge of the doctrine, of the kingdom of heaven, should, from particular evidences, be at all times able to distinguish between the clean and the unclean, the sincere and the hypocrite; and pronounce a judgment as infallible as the priest did in the case of the leprosy, from the tokens already specified. And as this binding and loosing, or pronouncing fit or unfit for fellowship with the members of Christ, must in the case of the disciples be always according to the doctrine of the kingdom of heaven, the sentence should be considered as proceeding immediately from thence, and consequently as Divinely ratified. The priest polluted or cleansed, i. e., declared the man clean or unclean, according to signs well known and infallible. The disciples or ministers of Christ bind or loose, declare to be fit or unfit for Church fellowship, according to unequivocal evidences of innocence or guilt. In the former case, the priest declared the person fit or unfit for civil society; in the latter, the ministers of Christ declare the person against whom the suspicion of guilt is laid, fit or unfit for continued association with the Church of God. The office was the same in both, a declaration of the truth, not from any power that they possessed of cleansing or polluting, of binding or of loosing, but by the knowledge they gained from the infallible signs and evidences produced on the respective cases.
entries.812e1e27d4e26aec6eb6c601a4c71a9bcc5e3893: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen4678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4679" type="x-p"/> If the leprosy have covered all his flesh, he shall pronounce him clean - Why is it that the partial leper was pronounced unclean, and the person totally covered with the disease clean? This was probably owing to a different species or stage of the disease; the partial disease was contagious, the total not contagious. That there are two different species or degrees of the same disease described here, is sufficiently evident. In one, the body was all covered with a white enamelled scurf; in the other, there was a quick raw flesh in the risings. On this account the one might be deemed unclean, i. e., contagious, the other not; for contact with the quick raw flesh would be more likely to communicate the disease than the touch of the hard dry scurf. The ichor proceeding from the former, when brought into contact with the flesh of another, would soon be taken into the constitution by means of the absorbent vessels; but where the whole surface was perfectly dry, the absorbent vessels of another person coming in contact with the diseased man could imbibe nothing, and therefore there was comparatively no danger of infection. Hence that species or stage of the disease that exhibited the quick raw rising was capable of conveying the infection for the reasons already assigned, when the other was not. Dr. Mead thus accounts for the circumstance mentioned in the text. See on <reference osisRef="Lev.13.18">Lev 13:18</reference> (note). As the leprosy infected bodies, clothes, and even the walls of houses, is it not rational to suppose that it was occasioned by a species of animalcula or vermin burrowing under the skin? Of this opinion there are some learned supporters.
entries.5b9b5e02e607cbcf6bfc37c37055bf42615c2c82: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen4679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4680" type="x-p"/> In the skin thereof, was a boil - Scheuchzer supposes this and the following verse to speak of phlegmonic, erysipelatous, gangrenous, and phagedenic ulcers, all of which were subjected to the examination of the priest, to see whether they were infectious, or whether the leprosy might not take its origin from them. A person with any sore or disposition to contagion was more likely to catch the infection by contact with the diseased person, than he was whose skin was whole and sound, and his habit good.
entries.58624286e6f7755b0ef9d1836d78cb30cdac4a1d: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen4680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4681" type="x-p"/> A plague upon the head or the beard - This refers to a disease in which, according to the Jews, the hair either on the head or the chin dropped out by the roots.
entries.5504e06ab987b1d26f5448c4ae2eb209b289f39e: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen4681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4682" type="x-p"/> The scall shall he not shave - Lest the place should be irritated and inflamed, and assume in consequence other appearances besides those of a leprous infection; in which case the priest might not be able to form an accurate judgment.
entries.e48ed8c84539da96d25c94aad3b3aec642fdb59b: <hi type="bold">Verse 45</hi> <div eID="gen4682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4683" type="x-p"/> His clothes shall be rent, etc. - The leprous person is required to be as one that mourned for the dead, or for some great and public calamity. He was to have his clothes rent in token of extreme sorrow; his head was to be made bare, the ordinary bonnet or turban being omitted; and he was to have a covering upon his upper lip, his jaws being tied up With a linen cloth, after the same manner in which the Jews bind up the dead, which custom is still observed among the Jews in Barbary on funeral occasions: a custom which, from <reference osisRef="Eze.24.17">Eze 24:17</reference>, we learn had prevailed very anciently among the Jews in Palestine. He was also to cry, Unclean, unclean, in order to prevent any person from coming near him, lest the contagion might be thus communicated and diffused through society; and hence the Targumist render it, Be not ye made unclean! Be not ye made unclean! A caution to others not to come near him.
entries.dd2f07ceee37ab14b3f4807e0995cf9caf10a70f: <hi type="bold">Verse 47</hi> <div eID="gen4683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4684" type="x-p"/> The garment also - The whole account here seems to intimate that the garment was fretted by this contagion; and hence it is likely that it was occasioned by a species of small animals, which we know to be the cause of the itch; these, by breeding in the garments, must necessarily multiply their kind, and fret the garments, i. e., corrode a, portion of the finer parts, after the manner of moths, for their nourishment. See <reference osisRef="Lev.13.52">Lev 13:52</reference> (note).
entries.5aff278b5f20c3e192a634e126376dc78ec86e27: <hi type="bold">Verse 52</hi> <div eID="gen4684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4685" type="x-p"/> He shall therefore burn that garment - There being scarcely any means of radically curing the infection. It is well known that the garments infected by the psora, or itch animal, have been known to communicate the disease even six or seven years after the first infection. This has been also experienced by the sorters of rags at some paper mills.
entries.dd01252e4002aa604124ff3215dbf97cbaf3f463: <hi type="bold">Verse 54</hi> <div eID="gen4685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4686" type="x-p"/> He shall shut it up seven days more - To give time for the spreading of the contagion, if it did exist there; that there might be the most unequivocal marks and proofs that the garment was or was not infected.
entries.ad425efbaebf6bb4419407bb366597f1b1009364: <hi type="bold">Verse 58</hi> <div eID="gen4686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4687" type="x-p"/> It shall be washed the second time - According to the Jews the first washing was to put away the plague, the second to cleanse it. Both among Jews and Gentiles the leprosy has been considered as a most expressive emblem of sin, the properties and circumstances of the one pointing out those of the other. The similitude or parallel has been usually run in the following manner: - <div eID="gen4687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4688" type="x-p"/> 1. The leprosy began with a spot, a simple hidden infection being the cause. <div eID="gen4688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4689" type="x-p"/> 2. This spot was very conspicuous, and argued the source whence it proceeded. <div eID="gen4689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4690" type="x-p"/> 3. It was of a diffusive nature, soon spreading over the whole body. <div eID="gen4690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4691" type="x-p"/> 4. It communicated its infectious nature, not only to the whole of the person's body, but also to his clothes and habitation. <div eID="gen4691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4692" type="x-p"/> 5. It rendered the infected person loathsome, unfit for and dangerous to society because of its infectious nature. <div eID="gen4692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4693" type="x-p"/> 6. The person infected was obliged to be separated from society, both religious and civil; to dwell by himself without the camp or city, and hold commerce with none. <div eID="gen4693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4694" type="x-p"/> 7. He was obliged to proclaim his own uncleanness, publicly acknowledge his defilement, and, sensible of his plague, continue humbled and abased before God and man. <div eID="gen4694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4695" type="x-p"/> How expressive all these are of the nature of sin and the state of a sinner, a spiritual mind will at once perceive. <div eID="gen4695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4696" type="x-p"/> 1. The original infection or corruption of nature is the grand hidden cause, source, and spring of all transgression. <div eID="gen4696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4697" type="x-p"/> 2. Iniquity is a seed that has its growth, gradual increase, and perfection. As the various powers of the mind are developed, so it diffuses itself, infecting every passion and appetite through their whole extent and operation. <div eID="gen4697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4698" type="x-p"/> 3. As it spreads in the mind, so it diffuses itself through the life; every action partaking of its influence, till the whole conduct becomes a tissue of transgression, because every imagination of the thoughts of a sinner's heart is only evil continually, Genesis 6. This is the natural state of man. <div eID="gen4698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4699" type="x-p"/> 4. As a sinner is infected, so is he infectious; by his precept and example he spreads the infernal contagion wherever he goes; joining with the multitude to do evil, strengthening and being strengthened in the ways of sin and death, and becoming especially a snare and a curse to his own household. <div eID="gen4699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4700" type="x-p"/> 5. That a sinner is abominable in the sight of God and of all good men, that he is unfit for the society of the righteous, and that he cannot, as such, be admitted into the kingdom of God, needs no proof. <div eID="gen4700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4701" type="x-p"/> 6. It is owing to the universality of the evil that sinners are not expelled from society as the most dangerous of all monsters, and obliged to live without having any commerce with their fellow creatures. Ten lepers could associate together, because partaking of the same infection: and civil society is generally maintained, because composed of a leprous community. <div eID="gen4701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4702" type="x-p"/> 7. He that wishes to be saved from his sins must humble himself before God and man, sensible of his own sore and the plague of his heart; confess his transgressions; look to God for a cure, from whom alone it can be received; and bring that Sacrifice by which alone the guilt can be taken away, and his soul be purified from all unrighteousness. See the conclusion of the following chapter at <reference osisRef="Lev.14.53">Lev 14:53</reference> (note).  <chapter eID="Lev.13"/> <div eID="gen4702" type="x-p"/>

entries.822264e7a618edffc04d09a80990535c8b2b1993: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.1">Lev 13:1</reference> <div eID="gen1308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1309" type="x-p"/> Leprosy. - The law for leprosy, the observance of which is urged upon the people again in <reference osisRef="Deut.24.8-Deut.24.9">Deu 24:8-9</reference>, treats, in the <hi type="italic">first</hi> place, of leprosy in men: (<hi type="italic">a</hi>) in its dangerous forms when appearing either on the skin (vv. 2-28), or on the head and beard (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.29-Lev.13.37">Lev 13:29-37</reference>); (<hi type="italic">b</hi>) in harmless forms (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.38">Lev 13:38</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.13.39">Lev 13:39</reference>); and (<hi type="italic">c</hi>) when appearing on a bald head (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.40-Lev.13.44">Lev 13:40-44</reference>). To this there are added instructions for the removal of the leper from the society of other men (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.45">Lev 13:45</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.13.46">Lev 13:46</reference>). It treats, <hi type="italic">secondly</hi>, of leprosy in linen, woollen, and leather articles, and the way to treat them (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.47-Lev.13.59">Lev 13:47-59</reference>); <hi type="italic">thirdly</hi>, of the purification of persons recovered from leprosy (<reference osisRef="Lev.14.1-Lev.14.32">Lev 14:1-32</reference>); and <hi type="italic">fourthly</hi>, of leprosy in houses and the way to remove it (vv. 33-53). - The laws for leprosy in man relate exclusively to the so-called white leprosy, λεύκη λέπρα, <hi type="italic">lepra</hi>, which probably existed at that time in hither Asia alone, not only among the Israelites and Jews (Num 12:10.; <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.29">2Sa 3:29</reference>; 2Ki 5:27; 2Ki 7:3; 2Ki 15:5; <reference osisRef="Matt.8.2-Matt.8.3">Mat 8:2-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.10.8">Mat 10:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.11.5">Mat 11:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.26.6">Mat 26:6</reference>, etc.), but also among the Syrians (2Ki 5:1.), and which is still found in that part of the world, most frequently in the countries of the Lebanon and Jordan and in the neighbourhood of Damascus, in which city there are three hospitals for lepers (<hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, pp. 277, 278), and occasionally in Arabia (<hi type="italic">Niebuhr, Arab.</hi> pp. 135ff.) and Egypt; though at the present time the pimply leprosy, <hi type="italic">lepra tuberosa s. articulorum</hi> (the leprosy of the joints), is more prevalent in the East, and frequently occurs in Egypt in the lower extremities in the form of elephantiasis. Of the white leprosy (called <hi type="italic">Lepra Mosaica</hi>), which is still met with in Arabia sometimes, where it is called <hi type="italic">Baras</hi>, <hi type="italic">Trusen</hi> gives the following description: “Very frequently, even for years before the actual outbreak of the disease itself, white, yellowish spots are seen lying deep in the skin, particularly on the genitals, in the face, on the forehead, or in the joints. They are without feeling, and sometimes cause the hair to assume the same colour as the spots. These spots afterwards pierce through the cellular tissue, and reach the muscles and bones. The hair becomes white and woolly, and at length falls off; hard gelatinous swellings are formed in the cellular tissue; the skin gets hard, rough, and seamy, lymph exudes from it, and forms large scabs, which fall off from time to time, and under these there are often offensive running sores. The nails then swell, curl up, and fall off; <hi type="italic">entropium</hi> is formed, with bleeding gums, the nose stopped up, and a considerable flow of saliva... The senses become dull, the patient gets thin and weak, colliquative diarrhea sets in, and incessant thirst and burning fever terminate his sufferings” (<hi type="italic">Krankheiten d. alten Hebr. </hi>p. 165).
entries.990759deb38a8a1e93b67056f1ccac427a18721b: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.2-Lev.13.28">Lev 13:2-28</reference> <hi type="italic">The symptoms of leprosy, whether proceeding directly from eruptions in the skin, or caused by a boil or burn</hi>. - <reference osisRef="Lev.13.2">Lev 13:2</reference>-8. <hi type="italic">The first case:</hi> “When a man shall have in the skin of his flesh (body) a raised spot or scab, or a bright spot.” שׂאת, a lifting up (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.7">Gen 4:7</reference>, etc.), signifies here an elevation of the skin in some part of the body, a raised spot like a pimple. ספּחת, an eruption, scurf, or scab, from ספח to pour out, “a pouring out as it were from the flesh or skin” (<hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>). בּהרת .)le, from בּהר, in the Arabic and Chaldee to shine, is a bright swollen spot in the skin. If ether of these signs became “a spot of leprosy,” the person affected was to be brought to the priest, that he might examine the complaint. The term <hi type="italic">zaraath</hi>, from an Arabic word signifying to strike down or scourge, is applied to leprosy as a scourge of God, and in the case of men it always denotes the white leprosy, which the Arabs call <hi type="italic">baras</hi>. נגע, a stroke (lit., “stroke of leprosy”), is applied not only to the spot attacked by the leprosy, the leprous mole (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.3">Lev 13:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.29-Lev.13.32">Lev 13:29-32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.42">Lev 13:42</reference>, etc.), but to the persons and even to things affected with leprosy (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.4">Lev 13:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.12">Lev 13:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.13">Lev 13:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.31">Lev 13:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.50">Lev 13:50</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.55">Lev 13:55</reference>).
entries.d1e295d31c4e6871273dbf4131ac6ec3ba3e89a3: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.29-Lev.13.31">Lev 13:29-31</reference> <hi type="italic">Leprosy upon the head or chin</hi>. - If the priest saw a mole upon the head or chin of a man or woman, the appearance of which was deeper than the skin, and on which the hair was yellow (צהב golden, reddish, fox-colour) and thin, he was to regard it as נתק. Leprosy on the head or chin is called נתק, probably from נתק to pluck or tear, from its plucking out the hair, or causing it to fall off; like κνήφη, the itch, from κνάω, to itch or scratch, and <hi type="italic">scabies</hi>, from <hi type="italic">scabere</hi>. But if he did not observe these two symptoms, if there was no depression of the skin, and the hair was black and not yellow, he was to shut up the person affected for seven days. In בּו אין שׁחר (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.31">Lev 13:31</reference>) there is certainly an error of the text: either שׁחר must be retained and אין dropped, or שׁהר must be altered into צהב, according to Lev 13:37. The latter is probably the better of the two.
entries.e82cdebdc5dab9d13862adb878d73fbca4ef6a2e: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.32-Lev.13.34">Lev 13:32-34</reference> <div eID="gen1318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1319" type="x-p"/> If the mole had not spread by that time, and the two signs mentioned were not discernible, the person affected was to shave himself, but not to shave the nethek, the eruption or scurfy place, and the priest was to shut him up for seven days more, and then to look whether any alteration had taken place; and if not, to pronounce him clean, whereupon he was to wash his clothes (see <reference osisRef="Lev.13.6">Lev 13:6</reference>).
entries.5168e86519494aaa970c5e995f0b8ed2bfecaa4d: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.35-Lev.13.36">Lev 13:35-36</reference> <div eID="gen1319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1320" type="x-p"/> But if the eruption spread even after his purification, the priest, on seeing this, was not to look for yellow hair. “He is unclean:” that is to say, he was to pronounce him unclean without searching for yellow hairs; the spread of the eruption was a sufficient proof of the leprosy.
entries.0f387982decddcf084800acc3af41b83c7457a4d: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.37">Lev 13:37</reference> <div eID="gen1320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1321" type="x-p"/> But if, on the contrary, the eruption stood (see <reference osisRef="Lev.13.5">Lev 13:5</reference>), and black hair grew out of it, he was healed, and the person affected was to be declared clean.
entries.64a8aa98e21ed20bec9e9980b27525ce5264361c: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.38-Lev.13.39">Lev 13:38-39</reference> <hi type="italic">Harmless leprosy</hi>. - This broke out upon the skin of the body in בּהרת plaits, “white rings.” If these were dull or a pale white, it was the harmless <hi type="italic">bohak</hi>, ἀλφός (lxx), which did not defile, and which even the Arabs, who still call it <hi type="italic">bahak</hi>, consider harmless. It is an eruption upon the skin, appearing in somewhat elevated spots or rings of inequal sizes and a pale white colour, which do not change the hair; it causes no inconvenience, and lasts from two months to two years.
entries.0b597269bf9d4c5492a14965ac045d19f2aa9530: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.40-Lev.13.41">Lev 13:40-41</reference> <hi type="italic">The leprosy of bald heads</hi>. - קרח is a head bald behind; גּבּח, in front, “bald from the side, or edge of his face, i.e., from the forehead and temples.” Bald heads of both kinds were naturally clean.
entries.a46e9ba9f29af5272ada639d26ba2cdf406149e3: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.42-Lev.13.44">Lev 13:42-44</reference> <div eID="gen1321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1322" type="x-p"/> But if a white reddish mole was formed upon the bald place before or behind, it was leprosy breaking out upon it, and was to be recognised by the fact that the rising of the mole had the appearance of leprosy on the skin of the body. In that case the person was unclean, and to be pronounced so by the priest. “On his head is his plague of leprosy,” i.e., he has it in his head.
entries.a5dac1b70dc22101c6273ab5b496fee042d5d967: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.45-Lev.13.46">Lev 13:45-46</reference> <div eID="gen1322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1323" type="x-p"/> With regard to <hi type="italic">the treatment of lepers</hi>, the lawgiver prescribed that they should wear mourning costume, rend their clothes, leave the hair of their head in disorder (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.10.6">Lev 10:6</reference>), keep the beard covered (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.17">Eze 24:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.22">Eze 24:22</reference>), and cry “Unclean, unclean,” that every one might avoid them for fear of being defiled (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.15">Lam 4:15</reference>); and as long as the disease lasted they were to dwell apart outside the camp (Num 5:2., Num 12:10., cf. 2Ki 15:5; 2Ki 7:3),<note placement="foot">At the present day there are pest-houses specially set apart for lepers outside the towns. In Jerusalem they are situated against the Zion-gate (see Robinson, <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> i.p. 364).</note> a rule which implies that the leper rendered others unclean by contact. From this the Rabbins taught, that by merely entering a house, a leper polluted everything within it (<hi type="italic">Mishnah</hi>, Kelim i. 4; Negaim xiii. 11).
entries.f161efe62ee93b9f6a0c0ffe05df7fd05c5f9335: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.47-Lev.13.52">Lev 13:47-52</reference> <hi type="italic">Leprosy in linen, woollen, and leather fabrics and clothes</hi>. - The only wearing apparel mentioned in <reference osisRef="Lev.13.47">Lev 13:47</reference> is either woollen or linen, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.22.11">Deu 22:11</reference>; Hos 2:7; <reference osisRef="Prov.31.13">Pro 31:13</reference>; and among the ancient Egyptians and ancient Greeks these were the materials usually worn. In Lev 13:48. שׁתי and ערב, “the flax and the wool,” i.e., for linen and woollen fabrics, are distinguished from clothes of wool or flax. The rendering given to these words by the early translators is στήμων and κρόκη, <hi type="italic">stamen et subtegmen</hi> (lxx, Vulg.), i.e., warp and weft. The objection offered to this rendering, that warp and weft could not be kept so separate from one another, that the one could be touched and rendered leprous without the other, has been met by <hi type="italic">Gussetius</hi> by the simple but correct remark, that the reference is to the yarn prepared for the warp and weft, and not to the woven fabrics themselves. So long as the yarn was not woven into a fabric, the warp-yarn and weft-yarn might very easily be separated and lie in different places, so that the one could be injured without the other. In this case the yarn intended for weaving is distinguished from the woven material, just as the leather is afterwards distinguished from leather-work (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.49">Lev 13:49</reference>).
