The signs of leprosy were, if the mole in the fabric was greenish or reddish. In that case the priest was to shut up the thing affected with leprosy for seven days, and then examine it. If the mole had spread in the meantime, it was a “grievous leprosy.” ממארת, from מאר <hi type="italic">irritavit, recruduit</hi> (<hi type="italic">vulnus</hi>), is to be explained, as it is by <hi type="italic">Bochart</hi>, as signifying <hi type="italic">lepra exasperata</hi>. הנּגע ממארת making the mole bad or angry; not, as <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi> maintains, from מאר = מרר <hi type="italic">acerbum faciens</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">dolorem acerbum excitans</hi>, which would not apply to leprosy in fabrics and houses (<reference osisRef="Lev.14.44">Lev 14:44</reference>), and is not required by Eze 28:24. All such fabrics were to be burned as unclean.
entries.48aad17150cd97e6ffa7c8c8b5c69e1351cc4101: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.53-Lev.13.55">Lev 13:53-55</reference> <div eID="gen1323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1324" type="x-p"/> If the mole had not spread during the seven days, the priest was to cause the fabric in which the mole appeared to be washed, and then shut it up for seven days more. If the mole did not alter its appearance after being washed, even though it had not spread, the fabric was unclean, and was therefore to be burned. “It is a corroding in the back and front” (of the fabric of leather). פּחתת, from פּחת, in Syriac <hi type="italic">fodit</hi>, from which comes פּחת a pit, lit., a digging: here a corroding depression. קרחת a bald place in the front or right side, גּבּחת a bald place in the back or left side of the fabric or leather.
entries.828b10de0f4058bf4e4906812ed27ccaeb90b254: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.56">Lev 13:56</reference> <div eID="gen1324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1325" type="x-p"/> But if the mole had turned pale by the seventh day after the washing, it (the place of the mole) was to be separated (torn off) from the clothes, leather or yarn, and then (as is added afterwards in <reference osisRef="Lev.13.58">Lev 13:58</reference>) the garment or fabric from which the mole had disappeared was to be washed a second time, and would then be clean.
entries.0aa3e903f26e64544576a332c50dc33b581a8c79: <reference osisRef="Lev.13.57-Lev.13.59">Lev 13:57-59</reference> <div eID="gen1325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1326" type="x-p"/> But if the mole appeared <hi type="italic">again</hi> in any such garment or cloth, i.e., if it appeared again after this, it was a leprosy bursting forth afresh, and the thing affected with it was to be burned. Leprosy in linen and woollen fabrics or clothes, and in leather, consisted in all probability in nothing but so-called mildew, which commonly arises from damp and want of air, and consists, in the case of linen, of round, partially coloured spots, which spread, and gradually eat up the fabric, until it falls to pieces like mould. In leather the mildew consists most strictly of “holes eaten in,” and is of a “greenish, reddish, or whitish colour, according to the species of the delicate cryptogami by which it has been formed.”  <chapter eID="Lev.13"/> <div eID="gen1326" type="x-p"/>

entries.78437ebb36fa2092c9ac17511e5566bafb3871f4: <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.13.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Lev.13.2" sID="gen9913" type="section"/> <div sID="gen9914" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi> <hi type="italic">When a man shall have in the skin. </hi>Since every eruption was not the leprosy, and did not render a man unclean, when God appoints the priests to be the judges, He distinguishes by certain marks a common eruption from the leprosy; and then subjoins the difference between the various kinds of leprosy. For the disease was not always incurable; but, only when the blood was altogether corrupted, so that the skin itself had become hardened by its corrosion, or swollen by its diseased state. This, then, must be observed in the first place, that the Greek and Latin word <hi type="italic">lepra, </hi>and the Hebrew <foreign xml:lang="he">צרעת</foreign> <hi type="italic">tzaragmath, </hi>extend further than to the incurable disease, which medical men call <hi type="italic">elephantiasis</hi> <note n="4"> <div sID="gen9915" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="fr">Ladrerie</foreign> — <hi type="italic">Fr</hi>.<div eID="gen9915" type="x-p"/> </note> both on account of the hardness of the skin, and also its mottled color; not, however, that there is an entire agreement between the thickness of the man’s skin and that of an elephant, but because this disease produces insensibility of the skin. This the Greeks call <foreign xml:lang="el">Ψώρα</foreign>, and if it be not a kind of leprosy, it is nearly allied to it. Thus we see that there was a distinction between the <hi type="italic">scab </hi>and leprosy; just as now-a-days, if it were necessary to judge respecting the itch, (which is commonly called the disease of St. Menanus, <note n="5"> <div sID="gen9916" type="x-p"/> St. Mehan — <hi type="italic">Fr</hi>. C. probably wrote Melanus. St. Mean, or Melanus, was a Welshman, who founded the monastery of Gael, now called St. Meen’s, of which he became abbot, and where he died. At his tomb wonderful cures were effected, chiefly of cutaneous diseases, especially “itch and scab, to which a mineral well, which bears the name of the saint, and in which the patient bathes, seems greatly to contribute,” quoth honest Alban Butler.<div eID="gen9916" type="x-p"/> </note> the marks must be observed, which distinguish it from leprosy. But, as to the various kinds of leprosy, I confess that I am not a physician, so as to discuss them accurately, and I purposely abstain from close inquiry about them, because I am persuaded that the disease here treated of affected the Israelites in an extraordinary manner, which we are now unacquainted with; for what do we now know of a leprous house? Indeed it is probable that, since heathen writers knew that the Jewish people suffered from this disease, they laid hold of it as the ground of their falsehood, that all the descendants of Abraham were infected with the itch, and were driven away from Egypt, lest others should catch it from them. That <note n="6"> <div sID="gen9917" type="x-p"/> The reference here, I think, ought to be Josephus, Jewish Antiq., Book 3. ch. 11. Section 4. See also, “Against Apion,” Book 1. Section <hi type="italic">25, et seq. </hi>Tacitus, Hist. v. 3. Justin, 36. 2.<div eID="gen9917" type="x-p"/> </note> this was an ancient calumny appears from Josephus, both in the ninth book of his Antiquities, and in his Treatise against Apion; and it is repeated both by C. Tacitus and Justin. Yet I make no doubt that the <hi type="italic">Egyptians, </hi>a very proud nation, in order to efface the memory of their own disgrace, and of the vengeance inflicted upon them by God, invented this lie, and thus grossly turned against this innocent people what had happened to themselves, when they were smitten with boils and blains. But we shall see hereafter, amongst God’s curses, that He chastised His people with the same plagues as He had inflicted on the Egyptians:<div eID="gen9914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9918" type="x-p"/>"The Lord will smite thee with the botch of Egypt, and with the emerods, and with the scab,” etc. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.28.27">Deuteronomy 28:27</reference>.)<div eID="gen9918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9919" type="x-p"/>Whence it may be probably inferred, that God avenged the crimes of His ancient people with special judgments, which are now unknown to us; just as afterwards new diseases arose, from which those in old times were free. At any rate, Josephus, by clear and solid arguments, exposes the absurdity of this accusation, that Moses was driven from Egypt with a crowd of exiles, lest they should infect the country with their disease; because, if they had been universally affected with this malady, he never would have imposed such severe laws for separating the lepers from general society.<div eID="gen9919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9920" type="x-p"/>God first commands that, whenever a suspicion of leprosy arose, the man was to present himself to the priest; if any symptom of leprosy appeared, He commands him to be shut up for a period of seven days, until it should appear from the progress of the disease that it was incurable leprosy. That God should have appointed the priests to be judges, and those, too, only of the highest order, is a proof that His spiritual service was rather regarded than mere bodily health. If any shall inquire whether leprosy is not a contagious disease, and whether it be not therefore expedient that all who were affected by it should be removed from intercourse with others, I admit, indeed, that such is the case, but I deny that this was the main object in view. For, in process of time, physicians would have been better able to decide by their art and skill: whereas God enjoined this decision upon the priests alone, and gave them the rule whereby they were to judge. Nor did He appoint the Levites indiscriminately, but only the sons of Aaron, who were the highest order, in order that the authority of the decision might be greater. It was, then, by a gross error, or rather impudence, that the Papal priests (<hi type="italic">sacrifici</hi>) assumed to themselves this jurisdiction. It was (they say) the office of the chief priests under the Law to distinguish between the kinds of leprosy; and, therefore, the same right is transferred to the bishops. But they carry the mockery still further: the official <note n="7"> <div sID="gen9921" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="fr">Monsieur I’official</foreign>, etc. — <hi type="italic">Fr.</hi><div eID="gen9921" type="x-p"/> </note> the bishop’s representative, sits as the legitimate judge; he calls in physicians and surgeons, from whose answers he pronounces what he confesses he is ignorant of himself. Behold how cleverly they accommodate a legal rite to our times! The mockery, however, is still more disgusting, when in another sense they extend to the whole tribe of priests what they have said to belong solely to the bishops; for, since the sin under which all labor is a spiritual leprosy, they thence infer that all are excluded from the congregation of the faithful until they shall have been purged and received by absolution, which they hold to be the common office of all the priests. They afterwards add, that judgment cannot be pronounced till the cause is heard, and so conclude that confession is necessary. But, if they choose to have recourse to subtleties, reason would rather conduct us to the opposite conclusion; for God did not desire the priests to take cognizance of a hidden disease, but only after the manifest symptoms had appeared: hence it will follow, that it is preposterous to bring secret sins to judgment, and that wretched men are dragged to their confession contrary to all law and justice. But, setting aside all these absurdities, an analogy must be observed between us and God’s ancient people. He of old forbade the external uncleanness of the flesh to be tolerated in His people. By Christ’s coming, the typical. figure has ceased; but we are taught that all uncleanness, whereby the purity of His services is defiled, is not to be cherished, or borne with amongst us. And surely excommunication answers to this ceremony; since by it the Church is purified, lest corruptions should everywhere assail it, if wicked and guilty persons occupied a place in it promiscuously with the good. The command of God that, whilst the disease was obscure and questionable, the infected person should be shut up for seven days, recommends moderation to us, lest any, who is still curable, should be condemned before his time. In fact, this medium is to be observed, that the judge should not be too remiss and hasty in pardoning, and still that he should temper severity by justice; and especially that he should not be too precipitate in his judgment. What we translate “shall pronounce him clean, or unclean,” is in Hebrew, “shall clean, or unclean him;” thus the dignity of the judgment is more fully established, as though it had proceeded from God Himself; and assuredly no medical skill could declare on the seventh day a leprosy to be incurable, respecting which there was doubt so short a time before, unless God should in some special manner discover the uncleanness, and guide the eyes of the priests by His Spirit.<div eID="gen9920" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.13.2" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen9913" osisID="Lev.13.2" type="section"/>
entries.4041387d9967089558486fed5e5260d7b9a16b70: <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.13.29" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Lev.13.29" sID="gen9922" type="section"/> <div sID="gen9923" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">29</hi> <hi type="italic">If a man or woman. </hi>What is here spoken of is not the baldness which so often occurs in old age; but that loss of hair, which is the consequence of leprosy, is distinguished from any other, the cause of which may be some indisposition, and which yet does not pollute a man. But, inasmuch as some kinds of baldness do not so greatly differ at first sight from leprosy, — such, for instance, as <hi type="italic">ophiasis </hi>and <hi type="italic">alopecia</hi> <note n="8"> <div sID="gen9924" type="x-p"/> “Ophiasis, (<foreign xml:lang="el">ὀφιασις </foreign><hi type="italic">Gr.</hi>,) a disease, in which the hair grows thin, and falls off, leaving the parts smooth and winding like the folds of a serpent.”<div eID="gen9924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9925" type="x-p"/>"Alopecia, (<foreign xml:lang="el">ἀλωπεκια </foreign>of <foreign xml:lang="el">ἀλωπηξ</foreign>, a fox, <hi type="italic">Gr., </hi>the fox-evil,) a disease called the scurf, when the hairs fall from the head by the <hi type="italic">roots.</hi>” — <hi type="italic">Bailey’s Dictionary.</hi><div eID="gen9925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9926" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">"These </hi>regulations will be better understood from the fact, that the Orientals distinguish two sorts of baldness. The first is that which begins from the forehead, and the other that which begins from behind. The Hebrew has a distinct name for each of these. By the Arabian poets also, the former is distinguished as the ‘noble baldness,’ because it generally proceeded from the wearing of a helmet; whilst the latter was stigmatized as ‘servile baldness.’ With this understanding, let us read the terms ‘bald’ <foreign xml:lang="he">קרח</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">kareach</hi>) in verse 40, and ‘forehead-bald’ <foreign xml:lang="he">גבח</foreign><hi type="bold"> (</hi><hi type="italic">gibeach</hi>) in verse 41. (See Michaelis, iii. <hi type="italic">285.</hi>)<hi type="italic">” </hi>— <hi type="italic">Illustrated Comment., in loco.</hi><div eID="gen9926" type="x-p"/> </note> — it is therefore necessary to distinguish them.<div eID="gen9923" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.13.29" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen9922" osisID="Lev.13.29" type="section"/>
entries.c5f024a7fd12f073ea25ba74e8f0f9e4e97be9a1: <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.13.44" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Lev.13.44" sID="gen9927" type="section"/> <div sID="gen9928" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">44.</hi> <hi type="italic">He is a leprous man, he is unclean. </hi>In the first part of the verse he says that the leprous man must be counted unclean; but, in the latter part, he commands the priest to give sentence against this uncleanness, lest it should be carried into the congregation. On this ground he says, “<hi type="italic">his </hi>plague is upon his head,” which is as much as to say, that he is sentenced to just ignominy, for Moses takes it for granted that God holds up to public infamy whomsoever He smites with leprosy, and thence reminds them that they justly and deservedly bear this punishment.<div eID="gen9928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9929" type="x-p"/>The two following verses contain the form in which the sentence is executed, viz., that the man should wear a rent in his garment, which is to be the mark of his disgrace, that he should walk with his head bare, and with his mouth covered, (for this I take to be the meaning of the covering of his lip;) and besides this, that he is to be the proclaimer of his own pollution; finally, that he must dwell without the camp, as if banished from communication with men. Moses here <note n="9"> <div sID="gen9930" type="x-p"/> Add. <hi type="italic">Fr., “</hi><foreign xml:lang="fr"><hi type="italic">en </hi>parlant de l’oster du camp</foreign>;” in speaking of putting him out of the camp.<div eID="gen9930" type="x-p"/> </note> refers to the existing state of the people, as long as they sojourned in the desert; for after they began to inhabit the land, the lepers were driven out of the towns and villages to dwell by themselves. I know not whether the opinion of some is a sound one, that they were enjoined to cover the mouth or lip, lest by the infection of their breath they should injure others. My own view is rather, that because they were civilly dead, they also bore the symbol of death in having the face covered — as their separation deprived them of the ordinary life of men. Where we translate “shall cry, Unclean, unclean,” some, taking the verb, <foreign xml:lang="he">יקרא</foreign> <hi type="italic">yikra,</hi> <note n="10"> <div sID="gen9931" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="he">יקרא</foreign>. He shall cry, or call out. Had it been passive it would have been <foreign xml:lang="he">יקרא</foreign> There is, therefore, no ambiguity as to the voice, except to such as deny the authority of the points, or read Hebrew without them. — <hi type="italic">W</hi><div eID="gen9931" type="x-p"/> </note> indefinitely, construe it passively, “shall be called,:” and I admit that in many passages it has the same force as if it were in the plural number. But, because the repetition of the word “unclean” is emphatic, it is probable that the word is not to be taken simply for “to call,” (<hi type="italic">vocare</hi>;) and therefore, I rather incline to the opinion that, by the command of the Law, they warned all with their own mouth not to approach them, lest any one should incautiously pollute himself by touching them; although their uncleanness was perhaps proclaimed publicly, so that all might mutually exhort each other to beware And Jeremiah seems to allude to this passage, where, speaking <note n="11"> <div sID="gen9932" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Fr., “</hi><foreign xml:lang="fr">en parlant des pollutions de la ville de Jerusalem, il dit que tous pourront bien crier, ‘Souillez, retirez vous, retirez vous</foreign>,’” in the speaking of the pollutions of the city of Jerusalem, he says, that all might well cry, “Ye polluted, depart ye, depart ye.” <hi type="italic">A. V</hi>. “It is unclean, (or <hi type="italic">Margin,</hi> ye polluted,) depart, depart,” etc.<div eID="gen9932" type="x-p"/> </note> of the defilements of the city, he says that all men cried<div eID="gen9929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9933" type="x-p"/>"Unclean; fly ye, fly ye.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Lam.4.15">Lamentations 4:15</reference>)<div eID="gen9933" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Lev.13.44" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen9927" osisID="Lev.13.44" type="section"/>

He has indeed subjected woolen garments and furs to the ravages of the moth, and vessels of various kinds to rust, and other corruptions; in fact, has surrounded the human race with rottenness, in order that everywhere our eyes should light on the punishment of sin; but what the leprosy of garments may be, is unknown. But its expiation under the Law admonished his ancient people that the must carefully beware of even external uncleanness, so as to cleanse themselves “from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit.” It has appeared to me sufficient to touch upon the sum of the matter, because it would be almost superfluous labor to insist upon the words, although I should be unwilling to condemn the diligence of                   <ns0:head>CHAP. XIII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 AND the LORD spake unto Moses and Aaron, saying,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 When a man shall have in the skin <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">For there was the seat of the Leprosy.</ns0:note> of his flesh a <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> swilling.</ns0:note> rising, a scab, or<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> bright spot <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Shining like the s<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

                        </ns0:gap>ale of <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> fish, as it is in the beginning of a Leprosy.</ns0:note>, and it be in the skin of his flesh <ns0:hi>like</ns0:hi> the plague of leprosy <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">A di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stemper most frequent in <ns0:hi>Egypt,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Syria,</ns0:hi> &c. known also a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mong the <ns0:hi>Greeks,</ns0:hi> who note that it was not so properly a disease a<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> a defilement or distemper in the skin, whence Christ is not said to heal, but to <ns0:hi>clearse</ns0:hi> the Lepers that came to him. And this distemper is here provided against, not because it was worse than others, but because it was externally and visibly filthy, and because of its infectious nature, that hereby we might be in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />structed to avoid converse with such vitious persons who were likely to infect us.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 17. 8. and 24. 8.</ns0:note> then he shall be brought unto Aa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ron the priest <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Not to the Physitian, because, as was now said, it needed not so much healing, as cleansing, and was rather a ceremonial pollution than a disease, and because it be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />longed to the Priest to cleanse him, and therefore to search and discover whether he was defiled and needed cleansing. The Priest also was <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>o admit to, or exclude from, the Sanctuary, and therefore to examine who were to be excluded. And the dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />covery of this distemper was not so difficult that it required the Physitians art, but the Priest by experience and the ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />servation of those rules might easily make it.</ns0:note>, or unto one of his sons the priests.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And the priest shall look on the plague <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) The sign or appearance of the plague of leprosy. And this change of colour was an evidence both of the abun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dance of excrementitious humours and of the weakness of na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture, as we see in old and sick persons.</ns0:note>, and the plague in sight is deeper than the skin of his flesh <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">For the Leprosy did consume both the skin and the flesh, as appears from 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 5. 14.</ns0:note>, it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a plague of leprosy: and the priest shall look on him, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> pollu<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> him.</ns0:note> pronounce him unclean <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>make him unclean,</ns0:hi> i. e. ministerially and declara<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tively, in which sense ministers are said to <ns0:hi>remit si<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>s, Mat.</ns0:hi> 16. 19. and to <ns0:hi>destroy</ns0:hi> nations, <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 1. 10.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 If the bright spot <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> white in the skin of his flesh, and in sight <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> not deeper than the skin, and the hair thereof be not turned white, then the priest shall shut up <ns0:hi>him that hath</ns0:hi> the plague <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">For greater assurance: to teach Ministers not to be rash nor hasty in their judgments and censures, but diligently to search and examine all things before-hand. <ns0:hi>The plague</ns0:hi> is here put for the <ns0:hi>man that hath the plague,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>pride</ns0:hi> is put for a proud man, <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 50. 31. and <ns0:hi>dreamers, Ier.</ns0:hi> 27. 9.</ns0:note>, seven dayes.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 And the priest shall look on him the se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venth day: and behold, <ns0:hi>if</ns0:hi> the plague in his sight be at a stay <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">This translation is justified by the following clause which is added to explain it.                      </ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> the plague spread not in the skin, then the priest shall shut him up seven dayes more.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And the priest shall look on him again the se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venth day: and behold, <ns0:hi>if</ns0:hi> the plague be somewhat dark <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Which is opposed to the white colour of the leprosy.                         <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> cleanse him.</ns0:note> pronounce him clean: it <ns0:hi>is but</ns0:hi> a scab: and he shall wash his clothes <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Though it was no Leprosy, but a scab onely: to teach us, that no sin was so small which did not need to be washed by the blood of Christ, which was the thing designed by all these washings.</ns0:note>, and be clean.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 But if the scab spread much abroad in the skin, after that he hath been seen of the priest for his cleansing, he shall be seen of the priest again.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 And <ns0:hi>if</ns0:hi> the priest see, that behold the scab spreadeth in the skin, then the priest shall <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> pollute him.</ns0:note> pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nounce him unclean: it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a leprosy.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 When the plague of leprosy is in a man, then he shall be brought unto the priest;</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And the priest shall see <ns0:hi>him,</ns0:hi> and behold, <ns0:hi>if</ns0:hi> the rising <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> white <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">To wit, with a preternatural and extraordinary whiteness, as <ns0:hi>N<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi> 12. 14.</ns0:note> in the skin, and it have turn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed the hair white, and <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Or rather, <ns0:hi>o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>
                        </ns0:hi> the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>opulative put for the dis-junctive, as hath been noted before: for either of these were signs of a Leprosy, and one of these may seem inconsistent with the other, the former sign of <ns0:hi>white hair</ns0:hi> supposing the skin in which the hair was to remain, and the latter of <ns0:hi>live flesh</ns0:hi> supposing the skin to be consumed by the Leprosy,</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>there be</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb</ns0:hi> the quick<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ning of living f<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>h.</ns0:note> quick raw flesh <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Which shewed that this was not a superficial Leprosy, but one of a deeper and more ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lignant nature that had eaten into the very flesh, for which cause it is in the next verse called <ns0:hi>an old</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>invet<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>rate</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>grown leprosy.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> in the rising:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:94" />11 It <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> an old leprosy in the skin of his flesh, and the Priest shall pronounce him unclean, and shall not shut him up for he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> unclean.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And if a leprosy break out abroad in the skin, and the leprosy cover all the skin of <ns0:hi>him that hath</ns0:hi> the plague, from his head even to his foot, wheresoever the priest looketh:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 Then the priest shall consider, and behold, <ns0:hi>if</ns0:hi> the leprosy <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e</ns0:hi>) The sign or appearance of the leprosy: or the scab is called <ns0:hi>a leprosy,</ns0:hi> because at first view it seemed to be so to the Priest and to other beholders.</ns0:note> have covered all his flesh <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">When it appeared in some one part it discovered the ill humour which lurked within, and withal the inability of nature to expel it, but when it over<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spread all, it manifested the strength of nature conquering the distemper and purging out the ill humours into the outward parts.</ns0:note>, he shall pronounce <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> clean <ns0:hi>that hath</ns0:hi> the plague: it is all turned white: he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> clean:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 But when the raw flesh appeareth in him <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Or rather, <ns0:hi>in it, i. e.</ns0:hi> in the place where the sign or appear<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ance of leprosy was, when the flesh was partly changed into a whiter colour, and partly kept its natural colour, this variety of colours was an evidence of the leprosy, as one and the same co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lour continuing was a sign of soundness.</ns0:note>, he shall be unclean.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And the priest shall see the raw flesh, and pronounce him to be unclean: <ns0:hi>for</ns0:hi> the raw flesh <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> unclean <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">This is repeated again and again, because raw or living flesh might rather seem a sign of soundness, and the Priest might easily be deceived by it, and therefore he was more nar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rowly to look into it and to observe the place and manner and other circumstances in which it appeared.</ns0:note>: it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a leprosy.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 Or if the raw flesh turn again, and be changed unto white <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">As it is usual with sores, when they begin to be healed, the skin, which is white, coming upon the flesh.</ns0:note> he shall come unto the priest:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 And the priest shall see him: and behold, <ns0:hi>if</ns0:hi> the plague be turned into white, then the priest shall pronounce <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> clean <ns0:hi>that hath</ns0:hi> the plague: he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> clean.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 The flesh also, in which, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> in the skin thereof was a bile, and is healed:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And in the place of the bile there be a white rising, or a bright spot white, and somewhat red<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dish <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) White mixed with red, as when blood and milk are mixed together. A late learned writer renders the words thus, <ns0:hi>white and very bright</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>light,</ns0:hi> which indeed is the true colour of leprosy, to wit, when it is in its perfection, as <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 4. 6. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> But here it was onely beginning and arising out of a bile, in which together with the white, which was the colour of the leprosy, there might be some mixture of redness arising from the bile, o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> that part of it which was not yet turned into the nature and colour of leprosy.</ns0:note>, and it be shewed to the priest:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 And if when the priest seeth it, behold, it <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> in sight lower than the skin, and the hair there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />of be turned white, the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a plague of leprosy broken out of the bile.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 But if the priest look on it and behold, <ns0:hi>there be</ns0:hi> no white hairs therein, and if it <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> not lower than the skin, but <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> somewhat dark <ns0:note n="‖" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>and be contracted<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>

                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And if it spread much abroad in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean; it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a plague <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>the plague,</ns0:hi> to wit, of Leprosy, of which he is speaking.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 But if the bright spot stay in his p<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> spread not, it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a burning bile, and the priest shall pronounce him clean.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 Or if there be <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> flesh in the skin, whereof <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> a <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> a <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> ing of fire.</ns0:note> hot burning <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>a burning of fire,</ns0:hi> by the touch of any hot iron, or burning coals, which doth naturally and usually make an ulcer or sore in which the following spot is.</ns0:note>, and the quick <ns0:hi>flesh</ns0:hi> that burneth have a white bright spot, somewhat red<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dish or white <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Or, onely white, without any mixture of red in it.                   <ns0:p n="25">25 Then the priest shall look upon it: and be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hold, <ns0:hi>if</ns0:hi> the hair in the bright spot be turned white, and it <ns0:hi>be in</ns0:hi> sight deeper than the skin, it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a leprosy broken out of the burning: where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the plague of leprosy.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="27">27 And the priest shall look upon him the se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venth day: <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> if it be spread much abroad in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clean, it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the plague of leprosy.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 And if the bright spot stay in his place, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> spread not in the skin, but it <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> somewhat dark, it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a rising of the burning, and the priest shall pronounce him clean: for it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> an inflammation of the burning <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) arising from the burning mentioned, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 24.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                     </ns0:note>, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a dry scall, <ns0:hi>e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven</ns0:hi> a leprosy upon the head, or beard.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 And if the priest look on the plague of the scall, and behold, it <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> not in fight deeper than the skin, and <ns0:hi>that there is</ns0:hi> no black hair in it <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">For had that appeared, it had ended the doubt, the black hair being a sign of soundness and strength of nature, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 37. as the yellow hair was a sign of unsoundness.</ns0:note>: then the priest shall shut up <ns0:hi>him that hath</ns0:hi> the plague of the scall, seven dayes.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">32 And in the seventh day the priest shall look on the plague: and behold <ns0:hi>if</ns0:hi> the scall spread not, and there be in it no yellow hair, and the scall <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> not in sight deeper than the skin,</ns0:p>

                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:94" />35 But if the scall spread much in the skin after his cleansing,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="36">36 Then the priest shall look on him, and be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hold, <ns0:hi>if</ns0:hi> the scall be spread in the skin, the priest shall not seek for yellow hair <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">He need not search for the hair or any other sign, the spreading or running of it being a sure sign of leprosie, with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out any other evidence.</ns0:note>: he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> unclean.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="37">37 But if the scall be in his sight at a stay: and <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> there <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> black hair grown up therein; the scall is healed, he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> clean, and the priest shall pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nounce him clean <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The truth of the thing, and not the sentence of the priest, made him clean, and if the priest had partially pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nounced one clean who was not clean his sentence had been null. And therefore it is a fond and dangerous conceit to think that the Absolution given to any sinner by a priest will stand him in any stead if he do not truly repent.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="38">38 If a man also, or a woman, have in the skin of their flesh bright spots, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> white bright spots,</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="41">41 And he that hath his hair fallen off from the part of his head toward his face, he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> fore<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />head bald: <ns0:hi>yet is</ns0:hi> he clean.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="42">42 And if there be in the bald head, or bald forehead, a white reddish sore, it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a leprosie <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">It is a sign that such baldness came not from age, or any accident, but from the leprosie.</ns0:note> sprung up in his bald head, or his bald forehead.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="43">43 Then the priest shall look upon it: and be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hold, <ns0:hi>if</ns0:hi> the rising of the sore <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> white reddish in his bald head, or in his bald forehead, as the le<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />prosie appeareth in the skin of the flesh,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="44">44 He <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a leprous man, he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> unclean, the priest shall pronounce him utterly unclean: his plague <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in his head.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="45">45 And the leper in whom the plague <ns0:hi>is,</ns0:hi> his clothes shall be rent <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">To wit, in the upper and former parts, which were most visible.                   <ns0:p n="46">46 All the dayes wherein the plague <ns0:hi>shall be</ns0:hi> in him, he shall be defiled, he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> unclean, he shall dwell alone, <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Partly for his humiliation; partly to prevent the infection of others; and partly to shew the danger of converse with spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritual lepers, or notorious sinners.                   <ns0:p n="47">47 The garment also that the plague of lepro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sie <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Leprosie in garments and houses is unknown in these times and places, which is not strange, there being some diseases or distempers peculiar to some ages and countries, as the learned have noted. And that such a thing was among the Jews can<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />not reasonably be doubted, for, if <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> had been a deceiver, as some have impudently affirmed, a man of his wisdom would not have exposed himself to the disbelief and contempt of his people by giving laws about that which their experience shewed to be but a fiction.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>whether it be</ns0:hi> a woollen garment, or a linen garment <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">These two sorts are put by a Synecdoche for any other garments.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="48">48 Whether <ns0:hi>it be</ns0:hi> in the warp, or woof <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">A learned man renders it, <ns0:hi>in the outside, or in the inside of it.</ns0:hi> If the signification of those words be doubtful or unknown now, as some of those of the living creatures and pretious stones are confessed to be, it is not material to us, this law being abo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lished: it sufficeth that the Jews understood these things by frequent experience.</ns0:note> of linen or of woollen, whether in a skin, or in any <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">

                  <ns0:p n="50">50 And the priest shall look upon the plague and shut up <ns0:hi>it that hath</ns0:hi> the plague, seven dayes.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="51">51 And he shall look on the plague on the se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venth day: if the plague be spread in the garment, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in a skin, <ns0:hi>or</ns0:hi> in any work, that is made of skin, the plague <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a fretting leprosie, it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> unclean.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="52">52 He shall therefore burn that garment, whe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther warp, or woof, in woollen, or in linen, or any thing of skin, wherein the plague <ns0:hi>is:</ns0:hi> for it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a fretting leprosie, it shall be burnt in the fire.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="56">56 And if the priest look, and behold, the plague <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> somewhat dark after the washing of it, then he shall rend it out of the garment, or out of the skin, or out of the warp, or out of the woof.</ns0:p>
